transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 53 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (VectorScale CTO), Evan Stone (VectorScale Lead ML Eng), Aisha Khan (VectorScale Platform)

Summary:
- Demo/walkthrough of Redwood behavior under persistent long sessions + bursty TPS and streaming backpressure.
- Focus on how KV cache eviction, batching, and graceful stream backoff interact with timeouts.
- Agreed next steps: pilot pricing, provide tuning snippets, run a hosted burst test.

Topics covered:
- Long context retention and KV cache eviction policies
- High TPS bursts and queueing/backpressure signals
- Streaming response backoff and reconnect semantics
- Timeouts vs soft-queueing vs canary fallbacks
- Security/compliance and VPC private pilot requirements

Action items (quick): see metadata above for ownership and due dates.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we have about 50 minutes, we're going to walk through the edge playbook for long sessions plus bursty TPS and streaming backoff. l et me know if I should slow down.
[00:18] Priya Patel: thanks, Maya. Quick context — we have a product that keeps multi-hour sessions per user for document review, and we see periodic bursts from indexing jobs that pump up QPS 5-10x for short windows. We're worried about streaming timeouts and context erosion.
[00:34] Luca Morales: cool, that's exactly the pattern we wanted to show. We'll demo both the hosted API behavior and then the Console Optimize suggestions for batching + quantization.
[00:47] Evan Stone: quick note — our 95th percentile request is often a 12k token context with a 6k prompt and trimmed history, so large KV usage.
[00:59] Aisha Khan: also need to validate that logs and audit events don't leak PII when we do the pilot, so SSO and KMS are must-haves.
[01:12] Maya Chen: right — we have SOC 2 and SSO docs, and KMS integrations for private deployments. I'll attach the attestation link after.
[01:21] Luca Morales: starting the demo now — first, long session behavior. We're emulating a 12k token session with rolling conversation and prefix caching.
[01:34] Speaker 2: (background) we also have a notebook link shared, i think it's in the chat — "edge-long-session-notebook.md"
[01:40] Luca Morales: yes link: https://redwood-demo/edge/long-session-notebook (demo-only). watch the KV cache hit-rate on the right.
[01:52] [02:00] Luca Morales: okay at t+0 we prime the model, KV cache grows, and responses stream as expected. at t+7 minutes we replay a chunk that forces eviction thresholds — note the throughput and latency bump. you can see the  tail latency — it spikes from 120ms to about 540ms as the runtime rehydrates the kv pages.
[02:21] Priya Patel: when you say "rehydrate" is that disk to GPU spill, or is it purely memory eviction?
[02:30] Luca Morales: good question. in hosted mode, we spill to local NVMe-backed cache if the model is quantized + rehydration path is enabled; otherwise, eviction triggers an on-demand recompute of KV slices. sometimes the transcriber will read it as K-V cash, which is funny.
[02:44] Evan Stone: so that's a hard penalty per request? we can't tolerate 500ms spikes for some flows.
[02:49] Luca Morales: for latency-sensitive routes, we recommend a two-tier policy: pin hot sessions to dedicated shards (if you have Dedicated capacity), or use the prefix-level sticky caching + eager prefetch via the Console optimize suggestion. that reduces the rehydrate window.
[03:04] Maya Chen: also, on the Console "Optimize" tab, there's a suggested config: target_batch=64 for conversational backfill, max_concurrent_streams=20, and kv_retention_ms tuned to your 95th session length. we showed numbers in the sheet.
[03:22] Aisha Khan: can you show the burst test now? that's our main worry — the indexing job will spike QPS for ~3 minutes every 2 hours.
[03:30] Luca Morales: sure — switching to the burst harness. watch the request queue and the backpressure metrics.
[03:36] [03:45] Luca Morales: starting a 10x burst. notice the request router starts applying soft-throttles and reroutes some traffic to a slightly cheaper model variant to preserve tail SLOs.
[03:58] Evan Stone: rerouting to a cheaper model — does that change outputs meaningfully? we need to keep deterministic behavior for a downstream reranker.
[04:07] Luca Morales: good point. we only reroute to verified-compat variants — think lower precision quant or a slightly smaller architecture with same tokenizer. we attach a score delta probe so you can measure drift.
[04:19] Priya Patel: what's the policy for fallbacks? automatic? manual?
[04:23] Maya Chen: default is automatic with a canary guard. you can toggle auto-fallback in the routing policy: fallback-mode = off | auto | manual. auto will try cheaper variants first, and if performance drifts beyond your configured threshold we fail open to a buffer queue.
[04:40] [05:00] Luca Morales: streaming-wise, when we detect per-connection saturation, we send a backoff frame to the client and escalate to reconnect advisory. the client SDK will pause for X ms (exponential backoff default) and attempt to resume with a resume token.
[05:18] Aisha Khan: does the resume token mean we re-send the whole context? that would be heavy for 12k tokens.
[05:24] Luca Morales: no — resume token ties into the server-side session state; we only resend the delta. but if the session was evicted we trigger a rehydrate path which is where the cost comes in.
[05:36] Evan Stone: what about websocket timeouts? our infra will drop idle connections after 30s.
[05:42] Maya Chen: you can configure heartbeat pings — SDK supports keepalive and chunked-heartbeat. if the connection drops but the server-side session lives in the sticky cache, client can reconnect and resume within X minutes (configurable retention). if not, you fall back to a fresh request.
[05:59] Priya Patel: you said retention is configurable — what's realistic for a multi-hour session?
[06:05] Luca Morales: retention has memory cost; for multi-hour sessions we recommend a hybrid: pin the active user's hot sessions for up to 90 minutes in-memory and checkpoint longer history to the KV cold store with faster rehydrate if flagged as "hot". there is a tradeoff: cost vs latency SLA.
[06:22] [06:45] Maya Chen: switching to Console Optimize recommendations — we ran your trace earlier and the optimizer suggested 8-bit quant + per-layer kernel selection, and batching tweaks. the net was about 25% cost reduction at negligible accuracy drop for your eval set.
[06:43] Evan Stone: that's promising — can we get the quantization config files?
[06:49] Luca Morales: yes, we'll attach them. note: model-specific. for some Llama variants we favor layerwise asymmetric quant, for others we do GPT-style group quant.
[07:05] [07:20] Priya Patel: security question — if we do a Private VPC deployment can we still use the optimize console or is that offline?
[07:28] Maya Chen: Private deployments have an optional control plane tunnel — the Console can push policy suggestions, but you can also run Optimize locally. for air-gapped setups, we provide a CLI packed artifact. we'll share the deployment checklist.
[07:41] Aisha Khan: and audit logs? we need immutable logs forwarded to our Splunk with customer-managed KMS.
[07:47] Maya Chen: supported. we stream audit events to your Kinesis/S3 endpoint and sign them with customer KMS; logs are redact-capable via the platform. I'll include the docs.
[07:58] [08:10] Luca Morales: back to backpressure details — the router emits three signal levels: ok, congested, and shedding. congested means queueing and delayed scheduling; shedding means we start applying soft-fallbacks and rate limiting.
[08:26] Evan Stone: what metrics do we surface so we can automate scaling?
[08:30] Luca Morales: Console exposes token-per-second, queued-requests, kv-hit-rate, avg-rehydrate-ms, model-variant-delta, and backpressure-level. you can wire alerts to your pager or auto-scale policies.
[08:46] Priya Patel: we want AI instrumentation into our ops toolchain — does Redwood expose an event stream or webhook?
[08:52] Maya Chen: yes, webhook + prometheus exporter; the event stream includes per-request metadata but PII redaction is configurable.
[09:05] [09:30] (Demo pause — network flapping noise, brief crosstalk)
[09:48] Speaker 3: (unclear) sorry can you repeat the rehydrate number?
[09:52] Luca Morales: typical rehydrate is 300-700ms depending on NVMe vs recompute; we showed 540ms earlier under heavy pressure.
[10:02] Evan Stone: that's too high for our interactive annotator. we might need reserved shards.
[10:07] Maya Chen: Dedicated reserved shards are the pattern most customers use: pin X GPUs to your tenancy for hot sessions, and we maintain KV residency. that reduces rehydrate latency to 30-80ms.
[10:22] Aisha Khan: cost delta?
[10:25] Maya Chen: depends on usage. Conservatively, Dedicated is typically 2-3x hosted for steady-state but saves on tail-SLO penalties and reduces token egress when you do heavy sessions. The Optimize tool will show a cost curve.
[10:41] [11:00] Priya Patel: let's talk about pilot scope — what do you need from us to run a focused 2-week pilot?
[11:07] Luca Morales: ideally: a representative traffic trace (preferably p99 spike windows marked), a 1-2 small evaluation prompt set, and an account admin to provision the sandbox VPC if you'd like Private pilot.
[11:20] Evan Stone: we can provide traces, but redaction may be needed.
[11:24] Maya Chen: that's fine — we accept hashed traces or synthetic.
[11:29] [11:40] (Customer asks about error codes)
[11:43] Luca Morales: on the API we surface error classes: ERR_QUEUE_OVERFLOW, ERR_TIMEOUT_REHYDRATE, ERR_STREAM_ABORT, ERR_AUTH. you can map them in your retry logic.
[11:55] Priya Patel: for ERR_TIMEOUT_REHYDRATE, what's the recommended client retry strategy?
[12:00] Luca Morales: exponential backoff with capped retries and a late-fail to canary route. example: initial wait 200ms, multiplier 2, max retries 3, after that route to fallback variant or enqueue. we'll add sample code.
[12:16] [12:40] Maya Chen: time to run a small live stress — Luca will start a test that simulates a 180s burst with mixed long-context renewals.
[12:49] Luca Morales: starting test... watch queued-requests and kv-hit-rate.
[13:03] (Test runs — audible keyboard clacking in background)
[13:18] Luca Morales: you can see initial congestion at 8s; by 25s the router increased batching to smooth tails; a subset of streams received backoff frames around 32s.
[13:36] Evan Stone: did we lose any partial responses?
[13:40] Luca Morales: clients saw transient incomplete chunks but all eligible streams resumed with resume tokens; no final responses were lost — we verify at the app layer.
[13:52] Priya Patel: what about billing for retries and rehydrates?
[13:56] Maya Chen: retries are charged per token emitted; rehydrates count as server-side compute and will count toward compute units in the pilot. for cost predictions, Optimize provides an estimate line item for rehydrate events.
[14:12] [14:30] Priya Patel: can we throttle indexing jobs at our side to smooth those bursts instead of infra-level fallbacks?
[14:36] Aisha Khan: we prefer to avoid changing upstream jobs if possible, but we could add a leaky-bucket in front.
[14:41] Luca Morales: we support client-side rate limiting and token-bucket shaping and also have a server-side surge admission policy — often customers combine both.
[14:54] [15:00] (Short pause)
[15:12] Evan Stone: one more advanced question: can we checkpoint long sessions to an external cold store and rehydrate only relevant segments on demand?
[15:22] Luca Morales: yes — the platform supports session checkpointing to your S3 with index pointers. Optimize can compute diff-aware checkpoints to only pull necessary KV slices. that'll save on NVMe hits but add small rehydrate latency.
[15:38] Priya Patel: if we adopt that, what's the operational overhead?
[15:43] Luca Morales: minimal — the checkpoint lifecycle is managed by the runtime; you configure TTLs and the retention policy. we recommend you run the 2-week pilot with checkpointing enabled for long-tail sessions to quantify tradeoffs.
[15:58] [16:20] Maya Chen: wrapping up — recap of agreed items: we'll send pilot pricing and security docs, Luca will share tuning snippets and run the hosted burst test for your traces, and you will share the trace and decide whether you want Dedicated pilot or Hosted with pinned shards.
[16:38] Priya Patel: sounds good. one ask: could we get a short doc that maps error classes to recommended client actions?
[16:45] Maya Chen: yes, we'll add a 1-pager mapping errors to retry/fallback logic.
[16:52] Evan Stone: timeline — can we start the pilot next week? we'd like to kickoff by 2025-08-12.
[16:59] Maya Chen: that's feasible, pending paperwork. I'll send the pilot agreement and the checklist.
[17:08] [17:30] (closing remarks)
[17:35] Aisha Khan: appreciated, this was helpful.
[17:39] Maya Chen: great, we’ll follow up. thanks everyone.

End of meeting.
